title: Kufanya mazungumzo kwenye ndege / Conversations at the Airport
bridge: In Swahili, unlike English, the verb 'kuwa' (to be) is often omitted in the present tense. For example, 'Ni kwenye ndege' means 'I am at the airport' without explicitly saying 'I am'. Additionally, Swahili uses a more formal tone in public spaces like airports, so phrases like 'Habari yako?' (How are you?) are common but should be used with respect. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'What’s up?' as they may sound too casual.
rule: In Swahili, questions at the airport often use the word 'wapi' (where) or 'gani' (which) for location or choice. For example, 'Ndege wapi unatoka?' (Which flight are you taking?). Greetings are essential; always start with 'Habari yako?' or 'Hujambo?' before asking questions. Use 'tafadhali' (please) and 'asamahani' (excuse me) to remain polite. Remember, Swahili sentences follow a subject-verb-object (SVO) structure, which differs from English’s SVO.

title: Kukabiliana na Mfanyikazi wa Hoteli / Interacting with Hotel Staff
bridge: In Swahili, unlike English, the verb 'kuwa' (to be) is often omitted in the present tense. Additionally, Swahili uses a system of noun classes, which affects adjectives and pronouns. Be cautious with word order, as Swahili typically follows a Subject-Verb-Object structure, similar to English, but with more flexibility. Direct translations from English may sound unnatural due to these differences.
rule: When asking for something at a hotel, use the structure 'Nataka...' (I want...) or 'Je, unaweza...' (Can you...). For giving information, use 'Nina...' (I have...) or 'Nime...' (I have...). Remember to use polite forms like 'tafadhali' (please) and 'asana' (thank you). Swahili adjectives agree with the noun class of the noun they modify, but at A1 level, focus on basic phrases and common expressions.

title: Kuchagua chakula / Ordering Food
bridge: In Swahili, unlike English, the verb often comes at the end of the sentence. When ordering food, you'll use the structure 'Ninataka [food]' (I want [food]), which is more direct than the English 'I would like'. Be careful not to directly translate 'Can I get...' as Swahili uses a different structure for requests.
rule: To order food in Swahili, use the phrase 'Ninataka [food]' (I want [food]). For example, 'Ninataka wali' (I want chicken). If you want to ask for something politely, add 'Tafadhali' (please) at the end of the sentence. For example, 'Ninataka wali, tafadhali'.

concept_examples.translation: I want chicken and rice, please.

common_error.explanation: Directly translating 'Can I get...' from English to Swahili is incorrect. Swahili uses a more direct structure 'Ninataka [food]' to express wanting something. Adding 'tafadhali' at the end makes the request polite.

title: Kupata Dawa / Getting Medicine
bridge: In Swahili, unlike English, you often use the verb 'kupata' (to get) instead of 'to buy' when acquiring medicine. Additionally, Swahili speakers typically use the word 'dawa' for medicine, which is more general than the English 'medicine' or 'drug'. Be careful not to confuse 'dawa' with 'majii' (water), as English speakers might mistakenly associate 'dawa' with a liquid form.
rule: To ask for medicine in Swahili, use the structure: 'Nataka [dawa]' (I want [medicine]). For specifying the type of medicine, use 'dawa ya [condition]' (medicine for [condition]). Remember, Swahili adjectives often follow the noun, unlike English where they typically precede it.

title: Kunuza kwa bidhaa / Asking for Items
bridge: In Swahili, asking for items in a supermarket often involves using the verb 'kuwa na' (to have) in a question form, which is quite different from English where you might simply say 'Do you have...?' or 'Can I get...?'. Swahili also uses a more direct approach with the verb 'kuwa na' followed by the item, whereas English might use phrases like 'I'm looking for...' or 'Where can I find...?'. Be careful not to directly translate English phrases, as this can lead to confusion.
rule: To ask for an item in Swahili, use the structure: 'Je, unapoza [item]?' (Do you sell [item]?) or 'Je, unawa na [item]?' (Do you have [item]?). The verb 'kuwa na' is used to inquire about the availability of an item. For plurals, add the prefix 'vi-' for nouns starting with consonants and 'ma-' for nouns starting with vowels. For example, 'Je, unawa na viazi?' (Do you have potatoes?). Remember, Swahili questions often start with 'Je,' which is equivalent to 'Is it that...?' or 'Are you...?' in English.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'Do you have...' without using the correct Swahili structure. Remember to use 'Je, unawa na...' followed by the item. Also, note that 'mkate' (bread) is singular in Swahili, so no plural prefix is needed.

title: Kufanya Safari / Taking a Trip
bridge: In Swahili, asking for directions or discussing public transport involves specific vocabulary and structures. Unlike English, Swahili uses a more direct approach when asking for information, often omitting the subject if it’s clear from context. Be cautious with word order, as Swahili is SVO like English, but the emphasis on certain words can change the meaning. Also, Swahili uses suffixes to indicate possession or location, which is different from English’s use of prepositions.
rule: To ask about public transport in Swahili, use the structure 'Je, unajua...?' (Do you know...?) followed by the specific question. For example, 'Je, unajua kituo cha basi?' (Do you know the bus station?). When giving directions, use 'Nenda' (Go) followed by the direction, e.g., 'Nenda kushoto' (Go left). Possessive relationships are indicated with suffixes, e.g., 'basi yangu' (my bus), 'kituo chako' (your station).

title: Kujifunza Kujua Watu / Learning to Meet People
bridge: In Swahili, greetings and introductions are more formal and structured than in English. Unlike English, where 'Hi' or 'Hello' can suffice, Swahili uses specific greetings based on time of day, such as 'Habari za asubuhi' (Good morning). Additionally, Swahili speakers often include the other person's name in greetings, which is less common in casual English conversations. Be mindful of the tone and formality to avoid sounding too casual or impolite.
rule: When meeting someone new in Swahili, start with a time-specific greeting like 'Habari za asubuhi' (Good morning) or 'Habari za jioni' (Good evening). Follow this with 'Jina lako ni nani?' (What is your name?) and introduce yourself using 'Jina langu ni...' (My name is...). Always use the person's name in subsequent sentences to show respect. For example, 'Habari yako, [Name]?' (How are you, [Name]?). Remember, Swahili greetings often include inquiries about well-being, so be prepared to respond or ask back.

title: Kunu / Ordering Drinks
bridge: In Swahili, unlike English, the verb 'to want' (kuataka) is often omitted when ordering drinks. Instead, you directly state the drink you want, followed by the quantity. Additionally, Swahili uses a specific structure for requesting items, which involves the word 'njoo' (come) or 'tafadhali' (please) to be polite. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'I would like' or 'Can I have,' as they don’t align with Swahili’s more direct approach.
rule: To order a drink in Swahili, use the structure: '[Drink] + [Quantity] + [Polite request].' For example, 'Bia moja, tafadhali' (One beer, please). If asking a question, use 'Nakutakiwa...' (I would like...) followed by the drink. Remember, Swahili is less formal than English in this context, so keep sentences concise and direct. Quantities are always placed after the drink name.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate phrases like 'Can I have' or 'I would like,' which don’t align with Swahili’s direct ordering style. Instead, focus on stating the drink and quantity first, followed by a polite request like 'tafadhali' or 'njoo.'

title: Kuanza Makubaliano ya Simu / Starting Phone Conversations
bridge: In Swahili, phone conversations often begin with a greeting followed by an inquiry about the other person's well-being, unlike English where a direct 'Hello' or 'Hi' is common. Swahili speakers also frequently use the phrase 'Hujambo?' (How are you?) as a greeting, which requires a response before proceeding. Be cautious not to skip this step, as it’s considered polite and essential in Swahili culture.
rule: To start a phone conversation in Swahili, use 'Hallo' or 'Habari?' as the initial greeting. Follow this with 'Hujambo?' to ask about the other person's well-being. Wait for their response before stating your purpose. Common responses to 'Hujambo?' include 'Njema, asante' (Fine, thanks) or 'Sijambo' (I'm fine). Avoid jumping directly to your purpose without this exchange, as it may be seen as impolite.

title: Fahari za Ukombozi / Emergency Phrases
bridge: In Swahili, emergency phrases often use more formal and direct language compared to English. For instance, the word 'saidia' (help) is more commonly used than the English equivalent 'help me,' which can sound less urgent. Additionally, Swahili speakers tend to use the verb 'koja' (come) in imperative form more frequently than English speakers, who might prefer 'come here' or 'please come.' Be mindful of these differences to sound natural and effective in emergencies.
rule: In Swahili, emergency phrases typically follow a simple subject-verb-object structure. The imperative form is widely used to give commands or ask for help. For example, 'Saidia!' means 'Help!' and 'Nitaa nini?' translates to 'What should I do?'. Remember to use the correct tone and pronunciation to convey urgency. Common phrases include asking for assistance, describing an emergency, or giving instructions. Practice these phrases to ensure clarity and effectiveness in real-life situations.

concept_examples.translation: There's a fire! Get out of here!

Nimevuka!' is more direct and commonly used in emergencies. Avoid literal translations and focus on learning the specific Swahili expressions for better communication.
